en: *Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sūtra*, Scroll Two (From "At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha first sat beneath the Bodhi tree" to the end of the precept against sexual misconduct).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhizhou of Puyang.
At that time, from when Śākyamuni Buddha first sat beneath the Bodhi tree until [the point where] heart-mind to heart-mind reverently receives [the teaching], he was filled with joy.
Regarding the "Upholder":

the commentary states that this is the first chapter, titled "The Section on the Precepts of the Mind-Ground Spoken by Śākyamuni in a Number of Dust-Atoms Equal to the Great Gate," which concludes the preceding narration.
From this point onward is the second [section], concerning Śākyamuni.

The Chapter on Explaining the Precepts of the Mind-Ground is divided into three parts: 1. The Preface to the Precepts of the Mind-Ground (from here down to "this matter should be studied and respectfully upheld"); 2.
The Main Exposition of the Precepts of the Mind-Ground (from "The Buddha addressed the sons of the Buddhas" to "there are ten grave rules of liberation"); 3.

The Conclusion and Exhortation for Circulation (from "The Buddha said to the sons of the Buddhas" regarding the forty-eight minor precepts to "receiving and upholding them with joy upon the crown of the head"). Regarding the first part, the explanation of the Precepts of the Mind-Ground:
The Introduction has two parts: 1. The Prologue of the Sūtra Compilers (from the beginning up to "the Buddha recited the Mahāyāna precepts of all Buddhas"); 2.
The Self-Prologue of Śākyamuni Buddha (from "He addressed the Bodhisattvas, saying: 'I now, every half-month... down to "the first purity").
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, having first sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained unsurpassed enlightenment—[the commentary states:
this is the introduction by the compilers of the First Council. It is divided into two parts:

first, the narration of the name and light of the precepts (from the beginning until "he immediately emitted immeasurable light from his mouth"); second, the narration of the assembly at that time listening to the precepts (from "at that time, one hundred million billion" until "they listened as the Buddha recited all [the precepts]").
The Great Precepts are [the source].
Regarding the one who attained unsurpassed enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree:
the commentary states that the phrase "at that time" refers to the manifestation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Buddha; this was received from the Buddha’s reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

It is said "at that time" because it refers to the turning back of the precepts; this explains the meaning of the "distinctive teaching" (*vibhāga-śāsana*) in which the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya* are not fused.
If one asks what is meant by "at that time," it means that within the Dharma there are no temporal divisions of the three periods;

in the single body of all Buddhas, which is an infinite body, and in the infinite bodies, which are a single body, within the equal *dharmadhātu*, they manifest the time of receiving the precepts for the sake of transforming sentient beings.

Furthermore, because it was at the time of the formulation of the precepts, it is said "at that time," which refers to the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). *Śākyamuni* is translated as "Able" (*néng*), which is his clan name;
*Munī* is translated as "Benevolent" (*rén*) or "Silent" (*jí*), which is his personal name. Thus he is called "The Able and Benevolent One" (*Néng-rén*) or "The Able and Silent One" (*Néng-jí*).
Regarding the Bodhi tree, as stated in the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions): within the kingdom of Magadha, upon the Vajrāsana, there is the Pipal...
Because the Bodhisattva in his final birth sat beneath this tree and attained enlightenment,
it is named the Bodhi Tree (the meaning of "Bodhi Tree," including its similarities and differences across the Mahayana and Hinayana traditions, is explained at length in a separate chapter, etc.).
Regarding "the one who has attained unsurpassed enlightenment" (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*):
the commentary states that "unsurpassed enlightenment" is divided into two levels based on the limits of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

The first level of the meaning of unsurpassed enlightenment is established at the point where the Buddha has exhausted all *paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa* (segmented birth and death) and reached the end of the dwelling-place of the triple world (*tridhātu-sthiti-bhūmi*). It is as follows:

In all the Tripiṭakas of the Hīnayāna, it is taught that after completing the practice of the six perfections over two asaṃkhyeya-kalpas and fulfilling the karma for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) during one hundred kalpas, one severs the fetters through thirty-four moments of mind beneath the Bodhi tree and attains Buddhahood;
this is called the "single-layered attainment of unsurpassed enlightenment. This sutra is not like that attainment of unsurpassed enlightenment. Why is that?
When this birth-and-death through transformation and the fundamental grade of ignorance are entirely exhausted, one sits beneath the Bodhi tree and achieves unexcelled enlightenment.

As it is explained in all the Eight Treasuries of the Mahāyāna, having transcended the fifty-one stages and abiding in the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbuddha*), the source is exhausted and nature is fully realized;
sublime wisdom alone remains, solitary and serene, forever separated from all phenomenal existence, vast and expansive.

Because he shares the same substance as the great void, his measure pervades the Dharma-realm, and his response fills the ten directions; therefore, it is said that he has attained unsurpassed enlightenment (and so forth).
This concludes the initial summary of the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa.

The commentary states: Regarding the phrase "the first binding," it refers to the moment when the Perfectly Awakened One attained the realization of the Way; his essence transcends the three periods of time, being without beginning, middle, or end, and without either binding or non-binding.

For the sake of those who should be delivered, he suddenly and instantaneously bound the inexhaustible treasury of precepts within the tranquil site of enlightenment (śamatha-maṇḍala). Therefore, it is called the "first binding" of the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa (the term *bodhisattva-prātimokṣa* is explained as previously stated).
"Filial piety toward one's parents, teachers, and the Triple Gem; filial piety is the dharma of the Ultimate Way. Filial piety is named 'precept' (*śīla*) and is also named 'restraint' (*saṃvara*).

The commentary states: According to the Confucian school, the interpretation of filial piety is "the constant pattern of Heaven, the righteousness of Earth, and the conduct of humanity"—this is how it teaches people.

Nothing is more excellent than filial piety; therefore, it is called "filial" (*xiào*). In the Mahāyāna of the Buddha-dharma, filial piety is explained as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Thus, the *Benyeyingluo jing* (Sutra on the Ornament of the Original Vows), in the lower fascicle, in the chapter "The Great Assembly Receiving the Training," states:

"To transform all sentient beings through loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity so that they all attain peace and happiness is called the 'precept of gathering in sentient beings' (*sattvasaṃgrahavastu-śīla*). Therefore, it is called "filial."
The explanation of the character "filial" (孝) by means of the four immeasurables corresponds precisely to this passage.
Furthermore, as the Mahāyāna sūtras clarify that there is nothing superior to the four immeasurable dharmas for generating the bodhicitta and realizing the essence of a bodhisattva:
parents possess the grace of giving birth to and nourishing one’s physical life, while teachers and monks possess the grace of nurturing the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom. Third...
The Jewel is able to fulfill aspirations in secret, providing protection, transforming delusion into liberation, and leading the ordinary into the sacred;

there is nothing greater than this for establishing the lineage of the Bodhisattva. Since this path is the path of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), it is called the Ultimate Path (*zhìdào*).
The four stages above are the realm of the Bodhisattva’s reverent offerings; the Bodhisattva should serve each one with the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).

Because one accords with [the Way] through these matters, it is said that one is "filial and obedient toward parents," and so forth. That which is called "filiality" is the essence of the precepts (*śīla*);

it is also termed "restraint," which refers to the characteristics of the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts. However, apart from the essence, there is no basis for the manifestation of the characteristics;
and apart from the characteristics, there is no means to express the various aspects. Although the characteristics differ, they all share the same vehicle.
Because of his impartial great compassion, great kindness, great joy, and great equanimity, it is said that he is also named "The Restrainer" (and so forth).
This refers to the emission of immeasurable light from his mouth.
The commentary states: Because the light of the precepts is immeasurable, it is called "Immeasurable Radiance.
Furthermore, this is the light of the Vajra-jewel Precept of One Precept, which is constantly recited by the Buddha Vairocana from the moment he first generated the bodhicitta;
because this light cannot be measured, it is called "Immeasurable Radiance. As for "mouth," according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is named...

The face-gate is itself the unsurpassed tamer; by means of the light of awakening, he awakens sentient beings, and only after harmonizing with their capacities and movements does he preach the precepts.
Since these are spoken from the Buddha’s own mouth, the principle of the light of the precepts is likewise luminous as it issues forth from the Buddha’s mouth.
Furthermore, that the Tathāgata now emits light from his face-gate signifies that this is the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground.
The fundamental source of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is such that those who practice according to the teachings will swiftly attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "Now the Buddha emits light to assist in the realization of the meaning of the true nature (*dharmatā*).
All you people should now know: join your palms with a single mind and wait; the Buddha shall rain down the Dharma-rain to satisfy those who seek the Way. Now, the Buddha likewise emits this light.
Furthermore, this Dharma-gate for assisting and inspiring all Bodhisattvas’ ground of mind causes them to practice it, awaken to and enter it, and swiftly reach the original source;
therefore it is said that it is the original source of all Buddhas and the root of practicing the Bodhisattva path—the root of the great assembly of all Buddha-sons.
This is the meaning of assisting in the opening of the original source (which is the same as the meaning of the Separate Teaching). Furthermore...

Next, according to the meaning of the Perfect [Nature], the explanation of the light of precepts is as follows: it is also called the "light with causes and conditions" (the text states that it has conditions and is not without cause;

thus it is light); it is also called the "formless light" (the text states that it is neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor black); it is also called the "light that is neither form nor mind" (the text states that it is neither form nor mind, which is its meaning);
it is also called the "light that transcends the two extremes" (the text states that it is neither existent nor non-existent); and it is also called that which "can function as cause and effect."

Regarding "Light" (the text notes that this refers to that which is neither cause nor effect): I respectfully rely upon this present sutra, wherein there are six different names, yet they are all but one—the light of the Vajra Jewel Precept.
Thus, immeasurable lights are each a single light, and immeasurable lights and a single light are non-dual and without distinction;
the self-nature-pure Vajra Jewel Precept is one and the same. I respectfully [affirm this].

According to the scriptural text, the light of the precepts (*śīlaprabhā*) is the fundamental source of all Buddhas, the root of practicing the bodhisattva path, and the foundation for the sons of the Buddha within the great assembly.
Thus, the sons of the Buddha within the great assembly should uphold, recite, and skillfully study it.
Following the Master of Tiantai, there is an explanation of the light of the precepts in six stages: first, intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*).

I. Radiance (The text states: "The fundamental nature of the precepts for all sentient beings is inherently pure; these are precepts that can be manifested, yet they remain unmanifested because they are shrouded by afflictions.

Second, the explanation of the name: "Radiance of the Precepts" is also called "the radiance of the precept characterized by faith. This means that when sentient beings within the six realms possess great karmic potential that moves and inspires the worthy and holy ones—whether through hidden or manifest means—they receive the Mahāyāna precepts, whereby their faith is awakened.

As the text states: "When sentient beings receive the Buddha’s precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas. One should always maintain such faith, for the category of the precepts is already fully complete. III. Radiance of Contemplative Practice.

(That is to say, through contemplation according to principle and practice according to the Dharma, one attains profound faith and understanding, obtaining various samādhis and dhāraṇīs; as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding the merit of sympathetic joy, these fifty people constitute the root of the great assembly of all Buddha-sons within this sutra.

4. The Light of Similar Precepts (*sādṛśa-śīla-prabhā*): This refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) who realize the light of the similar adamantine precepts (*sādṛśa-vajra-śīla*), thereby being able to contract and expand their illuminating functions.

As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The Bodhisattva, in his pure body, clearly sees all that exists in the world. This sutra says: "The root of practicing the Bodhisattva path is this. 5. The Light of Realized Precepts (*pramāṇa-śīla-prabhā*): This refers to the Ten Faiths and the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*).

The Bodhisattva’s ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*)—these forty-one positions each partially realize the radiance of the Vajra Precepts. As explained extensively in the *Huayan Guangshi* (Commentary on the Extensive Meaning of the Avataṃsaka), from the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) up to Equal Enlightenment, the light of these radiances illuminates the ten directions.

This is the sixth, the Ultimate Radiance of the Precepts (*niṣṭhā-śīla-prabhā*). This refers to the fruit of Buddhahood, the Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), which exhausts the source and fulfills the nature; the radiance of the Vajra Precepts, with its causes fulfilled and its illuminating function boundless and sovereign, is named "Boundless Light" (*ananta-prabhā*), awakening all beings.
Now, as for the emission of this light from the Buddha’s mouth, the text concludes by stating: "Therefore, the scripture says that the radiance of the precepts issues forth from the Buddha’s mouth."
The six meanings and six names are as previously stated, where the Buddha himself concluded:
"The light of the precepts (*śīlaprabhā*) is the original source of all Buddhas, the root of practicing the bodhisattva path, and the foundation for the great assembly of the Buddha’s sons.

Based on this, the interpretation of the light of the precepts through the six stages in their perfected sense is profoundly appropriate; thus, although ordinary beings and sages differ, [the principle remains the same].

The light of the naturally pure precepts is one from beginning to end. Furthermore, it is said that for all sentient beings, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas, the fundamental source of the precepts is the naturally pure nature;
this is the light of the causal nature of purity. From the light of the causal nature of purity, the light of the precepts of names arises;
from the light of the precepts of names, the light of the precepts of contemplative practice arises; and by means of the light of the precepts of contemplative practice...

One emits the light of semblance-precepts; by means of the light of semblance-precepts, one opens and distinguishes the light of true-precepts; by means of the light of true-precepts, one emits the light of ultimate-precepts.
Thus, although there is a beginning and end, it is in fact without beginning or end, because it is free from the two extremes.

While it is said to have a beginning and end due to the distinctions between ordinary and sage, delusion and awakening, though these stages of delusion and awakening differ in their sequence, they share the same fundamental source.
The light of pure precepts is one (the explanation of the precepts according to the Perfect Teaching is complete).
At that time, the great assembly of hundreds of billions of beings, down to those who recite the Great Precepts of all Buddhas as taught by the Buddha, [all attained realization].
The commentary states: According to the sutra text, although only about forty assemblies are mentioned briefly, the total number of the great multitude reaches one hundred trillion.
Regarding the eighteen Brahmā heavens:

The first dhyāna has three heavens: (1) Brahmakāyika, (2) Brahmapurohita, and (3) Mahābrahmā. The second dhyāna has three heavens: (1) Parīttābha, (2) Apramāṇābha, and (3) Ābhāsvara. The third dhyāna has three heavens:
(1) Parīttaśubha, (2) Apramāṇaśubha, and (3) Śubhakṛtsna. The fourth dhyāna has nine heavens:

(1) Puṇyaprasava, (2) Vṛhatphala, (3) Avṛha, (4) Atapa, (5) Sudṛśa, (6) Sudarśana, (7) Akaniṣṭha—also called Maheśvaradeva; these four [from Avṛha to Akaniṣṭha] are where ordinary beings dwell. Furthermore, there are five [other] heavens which are the [five] Śuddhāvāsa.

Including the abodes of humans, these are also called the Five Pure Abodes (*pañca śuddhāvāsāḥ*): first, the Heaven of No Affliction (*Avṛha*); second, the Heaven of No Heat (*Atapa*); third, the Heaven of Good Vision (*Sudṛśa*); fourth, the Heaven of Good Appearance (*Sudarśana*); and fifth, the Heaven of Limited Expansion (*Abṛha*). Furthermore, there is the Heaven of Non-conception (*Asaṃjñisattva*), which is the abode of non-Buddhist outsiders;
it is excluded here because they have not yet taken refuge in the True Dharma.
The six heavens of the desire realm are:
(1) the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, (2) the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, (3) the Yāma Heaven, (4) the Tuṣita Heaven, (5) the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and (6) the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

The Kings of the Sixteen Great Countries (as listed in the "Chapter on Upholding" of the *Ratnaketu-Parājitapṛcchā Sūtra*): First, the King of Kośala; second, the King of Śrāvastī; third, the King of Magadha; fourth, the King of Vārāṇasī; fifth, the King of Kānyakubja;

sixth, the King of Kauśāmbī; seventh, the King of Kauśala; eighth, the King of Kuru; ninth, the King of Kaśmīra; tenth, the King of Mithilā; eleventh, the King of Karakaṇḍa; twelfth, the King of Gandhāra; thirteenth, the King of Śātavāhana; fourteenth, the King of Siṃhala... [and so forth].
(15) the kingdom of Gāḍha; (16) the kingdom of Kāñcugaja; (17) the kingdom of Pāṭī; and so forth—each of these kingdoms has its own king, and thus they are called the sixteen great kings.)
"Joining the palms and listening with a sincere heart as the Buddha recites the Great Precepts of all Buddhas.
The commentary states: This is the prologue by the compilers; it indicates that the great assembly listened with a sincere heart until the Buddha had finished reciting the precepts.
He addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "I now [recite] every half-month, from the dharmas and precepts of the Buddhas down to the foremost purity.

This is the second part of the introduction, wherein the Buddha personally sets forth the virtue of the precepts; herein it is divided into two: setting forth the virtue of the precepts and exhortation."

[The section on] "Training" (from "Addressing all the Bodhisattvas" to "one should recite having trained well") consists of two parts: the sequence of the precept-substance and the exhortation to receive it (from "O Sons of the Buddha, listen attentively" to "the first purity").
Regarding the former, there are three divisions: first, the exhortation to recite; second, the elucidation of the virtue of the precepts; third, the conclusion and exhortation to train.

"In this present time, I myself recite the Dharma-precepts of all Buddhas" clarifies that these are the Dharma-precepts of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, and were not originated by me.

Because it was established [by the Buddha], it is said that one should recite it oneself every half-month; "now" refers to the present time when the Buddha himself recites the precepts, hence the phrase "I now.
Furthermore, as this is the time when the Buddha preaches the precepts in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, he says "I now.

This clarifies that even the Buddha—who occupies the position of the ultimate perfection of the fruit—constantly recites the Great Precepts; how much more so those below the stage of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*)?
Since those who do not recite and uphold [this] should [be instructed], it is said:

"All of you Bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds, including those in the ten stages of setting forth (*prasthāna*), the ten stages of nurturing (*anupālana*), the ten adamantine stages (*vajra*), and the ten grounds (*bhūmi*)—you Bodhisattvas should likewise recite the ten stages of setting forth.
This is because these are identical in name to the "Ten Abodes" (*daśavihāra*) in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*’s *Mūlakarma*, as all Bodhisattvas proceed from the initial resolution of the mind.
Having practiced the various perfections throughout many kalpas and abiding in the stage of the ten faiths, one is called an "outer ordinary person" (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).

Because this bodhisattva practices the Dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*) within a mind of faith and conceptualization, and because this mind of faith and conceptualization remains outside the principle of True Suchness itself, they are termed an "outer ordinary person.
From this point, they enter the first dwelling, the Dwelling of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*), and attain a semblance of True Suchness.
The *tathatā* (suchness) of this present, similar mind is able to further advance the Bodhisattva toward the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood—the ocean of all-knowledge;
therefore, it is called the "Ten Approaches. Regarding the "Ten Nourishments," the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra’s Fundamental Karma* names them the "Ten Practices" (*daśa-caryā*).
This sutra refers to them as the "Ten Nourishments" because these practices are able to nourish the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-body.
Regarding the "Nurturing of the Ten Vajras," this is the same as the "Ten Dedications" (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) mentioned in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra’s* *Mūla-karma*.
In this scripture, it refers to the state in which all bodhisattvas dwelling in the stage of dedication take all their merits and universally share them with all sentient beings;
their minds are like vajras, indestructible, and they vow to direct their thoughts toward the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment] together with all sentient beings.
Because it is named Bodhi, it is called the Ten Vajras (the Ten Grounds have been explained above).
Therefore, the light of the precepts issues from the mouth; having an object, it is not without cause. Thus, light upon light is neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor black;
it is neither form nor mind, neither existent nor non-existent, and is not a phenomenon of cause and effect.
The commentary states: This is the second section, which correctly elucidates the virtue of the precepts. It is the fundamental precept for the sons of the Buddha within the great assembly.

Regarding the phrase "light issues from the mouth" (as previously explained), it is because there is a condition and not a lack of cause. The term "light" refers to the Buddha emitting light for the sake of the great assembly of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis;
thus, it is said that there is a condition. This is because the Buddha has constantly recited [the precepts] since his initial generation of the bodhicitta.
Because this is due to the precepts, and because the light of the precepts issues forth from the mouth, it is said that the light does not arise without cause.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there was once a Tripiṭaka bhikṣu who, having preached the Dharma for many lifetimes, constantly emitted various fragrances from his mouth;
now, the Buddha’s mouth emits the light of the precepts precisely because he has constantly recited the Dharma and the precepts, thereby perfecting them.

Furthermore, regarding the light, it is explained that within the *śīla* of gathering wholesome qualities (*kuśala-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), there is the *prajñāpāramitā*, which is able to destroy the darkness of ignorance and give rise to the light of the *sarvākārajñatā*.
Therefore, it is called the "light of morality" (*śīla-prabhā*). Because it issues from the mouth, it has a cause and is not without reason;
thus [it is said] "the light... Now, as for this light of light being neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor black, this is the light of pure and wondrous morality.
Because it differs from the five colors and lights of the five directions in the mundane world, it is said to be "neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor black.
Because this light of pure and wondrous precepts differs from material forms and the limited mind, it is said to be "neither form nor mind.
Because this light of pure and wondrous precepts cannot be grasped through the two extremes of existence and non-existence, it is said to be "neither existent nor non-existent."
This light of pure and wondrous precepts is unlike the views of nihilism or eternalism that negate cause and effect;
it serves as the fundamental basis for practice for those who have first resolved to attain Bodhicitta, leading them even to enter the fifty-two stages.
Therefore, it is said that this is not a dharma devoid of cause and effect. Thus, it is summarized as "the fundamental source of all Buddhas and the root of practicing the Bodhisattva path."
This is the very foundation for all the sons of the Buddha among the great assembly (the conclusion of the discourse on the virtues of the precepts, etc.).
It is that which all the sons of the Buddha among the great assembly should uphold, recite, and study well.

The commentary states: This is the third section, which exhorts the great assembly to receive instruction from a teacher; "receiving" refers to practicing what has been taught, and "maintaining" refers to upholding it.
To recite the text is called "chanting," and because the mind is focused with single-minded concentration and free from all distraction, it is called "learning well" (and so forth).
"O Son of the Buddha, listen attentively... down to 'the foremost pure one'. The commentary states:
This is the second section within the Buddha’s own narrative, which describes the essence of the precepts and exhorts their reception.

This single chapter both concludes what precedes and generates what follows, thus containing two meanings. Because it belongs to the introductory sequence (*nidāna*), it is called "concluding the preceding"; because the purity herein [is supreme], it is called "generating the subsequent."
The essence of pure precepts serves as the foundation for the ten grave and forty-eight secondary precepts, because the precepts rely upon the essence and the essence is able to sustain the precepts;
thus it is called "giving rise to. As for "listen attentively," one listens with careful examination to ensure there is no error.

Regarding "the hundred officials," during the time of Yao of Tang, only one hundred official positions were established; therefore, the "prime minister" (chāngxǎng) refers to [the head of these officials].

The *zǎi* (minister) cuts [the sacrificial meat]; the *xiàng* (assistant) assists the transformation of the state’s words. One who occupies this position observes the brilliance of the state and is thus able to serve as a guest-king (*bīnwáng*).
Because he initiates [the ritual] at the proper time for severing and cutting, he is called a *zǎixiāng*.

As for the *bǐqiū* (bhikṣu), it is translated here as "beggar" (*qǐshì*), "destroyer of evil" (*pòè*), "terrorizer of Māra" (*bùmó*), and "upholder of the precepts" (*chíjiè*). *Ní* (bhikṣuṇī) is translated as "woman. Regarding the eight classes of ghosts and spirits who manifest as humans:
Regarding those who transform into humans, according to the Hinayana Vinaya, this constitutes an obstacle such that they cannot receive the precepts.

However, in the Mahayana, all eight classes of beings who transform into humans can receive the precepts provided they understand the Dharma Master’s words; these are all called "the foremost pure ones.

This is because receiving the precepts through the arousal of the bodhicitta transcends the five stages of dwelling (pañca-vāsa-bhūmi) and the two types of birth-and-death; therefore, they are called the foremost.
First is purity. Thus, the *Benye jing* (Sutra on Fundamental Karma) states: "Those who receive the precepts transcend the four māras and surmount the suffering of the three realms;
from birth to birth they do not lose these precepts, which constantly follow the practitioner until they attain Buddhahood.
Furthermore, if a Dharma Master is able to teach and transform a single person within a land, causing them to leave the household life and receive the Bodhisattva precepts—

To transform all sentient beings and cause them all to enter the Buddha-way—this is its meaning" (and so forth, concluding the reconciliation).
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "I have already finished explaining the ten *pāṭimokkha* rules; the forty-eight minor transgressions shall now be explained.
[The commentary] states:
This refers to the section on the precepts spoken by Śākyamuni, which is divided into two parts. The first part, concerning the ten grave rules, has already been concluded as previously described.
Regarding the twenty-four, forty-eight minor precepts, they shall now be explained. This section consists of three parts: first, concluding the preceding and introducing what follows;

second, correctly manifesting the characteristics of the precepts; third, concluding with an exhortation to practice and study. As for the first: having already finished explaining the ten major precepts, this concludes the preceding;
the forty-eight minor precepts shall now be explained, which introduces what follows. (The meaning of concluding the preceding and introducing what follows is complete.)
Regarding the second section, which explicitly reveals the characteristics of the precepts, there are forty-eight precepts that may be divided into five segments, as indicated by the text itself;
thirty-two and nine [precepts] each refer to their respective chapters in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Alternatively, following the original structural principles, there are forty-eight chapters.
These two methods of textual division may be adopted or rejected at one's discretion; for the present, it is appropriate to follow the five-segment division.

Because the text employs five sections of exhortatory rules, the first three segments each contain ten precepts followed by one concluding chapter of exhortation, while the latter two segments each contain nine precepts followed by one concluding chapter of exhortation;

furthermore, to these respective numbers of precepts, the three characters "initial," "middle," and "final" are added, and they are thus named: the Initial Ten, the Middle Ten, and the Final Twelve (the latter being nine).
Because there is no middle between the first nine and the last nine [the five sections are concluded].
▲ Section Ten: The Precept on Not Disrespecting Teachers and Elders. First Text. Seven Gates: 1. The Intent of the Prohibition;
2. The Sequence; 3. The Explanation of the Name; 4. The Requisite Conditions; 5. The Deficiency of Conditions; 6. Gravity and Lightness; 7. Pervasive and Obstructed.
Regarding the original intent of this regulation: a bodhisattva should only practice humility, reverence, and deference toward all sentient beings, let alone toward teachers and elders;
since there is nothing more egregious than the transgression of suddenly showing them disrespect or contempt, this rule was necessarily established. (The intent of the regulation concluded.)
Regarding the second sequence: once a well-trained disciple of the Buddha has obtained the precepts, they ought to extensively cultivate various practices.
As for the methods of cultivation, one must necessarily receive instruction from a teacher. If a disciple harbors contempt for their teachers, there will be no means of receiving instruction;

if there is no means of receiving instruction, one's practice will have no basis upon which to stand. Therefore, next, among the ten grave offenses, it is first prohibited that [one should not harbor such contempt].
This is the precept against treating teachers and elders with contempt (the explanation of the sequential meaning is concluded).

Third, regarding the definition of the name: when one harbors a light attitude toward teachers and elders, behaves with physical arrogance, and dwells in pride and delusion, failing to provide the necessary service and offerings that ought to be rendered, this rule was established to prevent such conduct;
therefore, it is called "The Prohibition Against Treating Teachers and Elders with Contempt."
[The explanation of the precepts is concluded. Regarding the four conditions for the offense, there are four:
first, the person is a teacher, an elder, or a virtuous person; second, one knows they are a teacher and so forth;

third, one deliberately gives rise to a mind of contempt or disrespect; fourth, one fails to show reverence and provide support through one’s body. This constitutes the offense. [The explanation of the conditions is concluded.]
Regarding the five deficiencies of conditions: if the first two conditions are deficient, there is a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) for both, because one must show respect toward all sentient beings;
if the third condition is deficient, one incurs a middling offense, because one fails to show respect in body and mind toward one's teachers and elders;

if the final condition is deficient, one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), because one gives rise to a mind of contempt toward one's teachers and elders. (The section on deficiencies of conditions concludes.)

Sixth, regarding the gravity [of offenses], there are four types. First, with respect to the object (*viṣaya*), there are three grades: first, toward the two teachers; second, toward senior friends; and third, toward one's peers.
Regarding these three objects, it should be understood that upper, middle, and lower offenses are committed accordingly. Second, with respect to the mind (*citta*), there are also three grades:
if one commits an offense with a mind of resentment or a mind of malice, it is an upper-grade offense; if there is no resentment...

Equanimity (*upekṣā*) consists solely of pride and delusion; this is the medium grade. The three types of indolence (*kausīdya*), forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), and [lack of clear comprehension] are the inferior grade.
Regarding the correlation, one should understand the relative gravity of these factors through their mutual interplay with the three preceding objects.

Fourth, regarding the actual phenomena (*vastu*), there are also three grades: first, being unable to sell one’s own body and so forth; second, failing to provide respectful offerings in accordance with the Dharma and so forth; third, [the remaining cases].
The three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—of not performing rites such as welcoming and seeing off can be understood [according to their lightness or gravity].
Seventh, regarding the conditions for obstruction or non-obstruction: (1) if it is pitch black at night, or amidst smoke, clouds, dust, or mist, such that one cannot recognize the other;
(2) if one is asleep while the other is awake; (3) if one is gravely ill; (4) if one has recently recovered from illness and lacks strength; or (5) if...
Sixth, while seated and preaching the Dharma, if one listens correctly to the Dharma and protects the speaker’s mind, there is no transgression whatsoever;

this concludes the section on general applicability according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śīla-sūtra*. If, however, nothing in this sutra is explicitly opened up [as a general rule], this concludes the section on general applicability regarding permissibility and restriction.

"If a disciple of the Buddha wishes to receive the rank of a king, or the rank of a Wheel-Turning King," it is explained that this is the formal commentary on the precept against showing disrespect to teachers and elders, which is divided into three parts:

first, one should initially receive the Bodhisattva precepts (from the beginning up to "the Buddhas rejoice"); second, having received the precepts, one should designate teachers and elders and provide them with offerings in accordance with the Dharma (from "once the precepts have been obtained" [to the end]).
It is right that once one has arrived, one should make offerings to them. Furthermore, it may be said: "This person is a son of the Buddha and should receive the precepts;

this person is a son of the Buddha and should follow the practice. (The summary states: To fail to receive the precepts when one ought to receive them, and to fail to perform the service and offerings when one ought to do so—this is the simultaneous regulation of these two precepts.
Third, the conclusion regarding the violation of the regulations (from "If it is not thus" to "one commits a minor offense" is as follows). Regarding the first section, there are two parts.

First, it clarifies that one should first receive the precepts (from "First, one should first receive the precepts" up to "one should first receive the Bodhisattva precepts"). Second, it clarifies the benefits of receiving the precepts (from "All ghosts and spirits" up to "all Buddhas rejoice").
In the first section, clarifying that one should first receive the precepts, three positions are briefly cited: first, the king;
second, the minor kings (*kṣullakarāja*) and various feudal lords; and third, those who hold the imperial throne but do not exercise sovereign power—such as the emperors of this country.

The sons of the Emperor, the enfeoffed kings, and the two types of wheel-turning kings—namely those of gold, silver, copper, and iron (each possessing a specific number of treasures and responding as previously described)—and the three classes of nobility comprising all civil and military officials:
these three ranks of honor are capable of both benefiting and harming sentient beings.
If they do not receive the precepts, the spirits will not protect them; by what majesty could they then command and lead?
"Because of all sentient beings, it is said that one should first receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
"All ghosts and spirits protect the king’s person until the Buddhas are filled with joy.
The commentary states: This second section clarifies the benefits of receiving the precepts; for by receiving them, the person conforms to the will of the Buddhas.

Because all Buddhas rejoice and satisfy the multitude of spirits, one obtains the protection of all ghosts and deities, such that one’s body and mind are free from all calamities and misfortunes, and one’s rank endures for long.
Having received the precepts, one gives rise to a heart of filial piety and reverence; even toward those who merely provide material support, one should act with respect.
The commentary states: This second section, which introduces the text on causing the preceptor to receive offerings in accordance with the Dharma, is divided into two parts.

First, the introduction stating that one should make offerings to the preceptor (from "Furthermore, the bodhisattva... down to "...and provide for him"). Within this initial introduction regarding the preceptor, there are three sub-sections:
first, generating a profound mind; second, viewing the person as venerable; and third, performing the ritual of respect. First, regarding the mind of filial obedience, [it serves to] repay...
"Filial piety consists in providing kind support and nourishment; practicing this with reverence is called 'obedience' (shun). (As stated at length. As for the mind of reverence:
carefully restraining the three karmas is called 'respect' (gong); welcoming, attending, bowing, and prostrating is called 'veneration' (jing). (End of the section on generating a profound mind.)
Regarding the sight of the *sthavira*, the *upādhyāya*, and one’s fellow practitioners, it is stated:
this second point concerns the "veneration of superior persons," which briefly enumerates six types of *sthaviras*.
These refer to those who serve as the leaders in all assemblies. Second, regarding the *upādhyāya*, ancient masters translated the term as "one who gives birth through power" (*li-sheng*).
Because the power of the Path arises from this person, the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang and the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Tang dynasty both transliterated the Sanskrit term *upādhyāya* as such;
this translates into Chinese as "Preceptor" (*qīnjiàoshī*), for it is this person who personally instructs the disciple.
There are three types: first, the ten precepts; second, the full precepts; and third, the bodhisattva precepts. The *Upādhyāya* (Preceptor) should carefully examine the various sutras.
There are two kinds of Bodhisattva precept masters: first, the hidden master, which refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
second, the manifest master, which refers to the human teacher who transmits the Dharma with its characteristics intact.

Because this sutra states that one should inquire about the seven obstacles from these two masters, the human teacher who transmits the original teachings takes Śākyamuni Buddha as his *upādhyāya*, and thus in turn takes the human teacher who transmits the Dharma as his own [preceptor].
The Upādhyāya also [attains this], and so forth. *Ācārya* is a short vowel in the Sanskrit;
it is translated as "Right Practice" (*zhengxing*), because this person corrects the conduct of his disciples. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle eight, states:
"An *ācārya* is one who possesses noble practice in the world. In the Tang language, these two characters have the same tone as the title of the Tripiṭaka Master.
He is addressed as *ācārya*, translated as "Preceptor" (*guifanshi*), because he establishes the rules for the disciple.

There are six different types: first, the preceptor of the ten precepts; second, the preceptor of the *karmavācanā*; third, the preceptor of dignified deportment; fourth, the preceptor of receiving instruction; fifth, the preceptor of dependence;

and sixth, the preceptor who bestows the bodhisattva precepts (and so forth). Regarding the four types of fellow students (*sahādhyāyī*): these are those who study the Mahāyāna together and have received [the precepts] first.
Regarding the Bodhisattva precepts, there are five types of "shared views":

those who study together within the Mahāyāna and give rise to right view from the true causes and conditions of the Dharma (as explained at the conclusion of the section on the meaning of right view within the precept against false speech). Sixth, there are those with "shared practice," such as Dharma friends among Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time whose minds act in concert.
Furthermore, "view" is also called "understanding-practice" (*adhimukti-caryā*), and it is also "progression"; these may be shared.
A teacher may not necessarily be the same, but one who shares the same view, or whose understanding is the same, or who practices the Mahāyāna path—such persons are all worthy of respect.

Furthermore, this interpretation also applies to those who understand and practice the Hīnayāna; they too are worthy of respect, because ultimately there is no distinction between the vehicles, as all followers of the Hīnayāna enter the Mahāyāna.

Thus, the Lotus Sūtra states: "Even though... (The full passage continues: "...if one has already attained the fruit of Arhatship, yet hears this Dharma and attains the Buddha-way, one should know that such a person is a true disciple of the Buddha.")
The teaching of the three vehicles is intended solely for the instruction of bodhisattvas;
yet, conversely, these bodhisattvas give rise to conceit, arrogance, and delusion—even toward those who provide them with basic support.
The commentary states that within this third section on the protocol of showing respect, such actions constitute a failure and a transgression, as they arise from a mind of pride and haughtiness.
Therefore, it is the opposite of the aforementioned mind of reverence; because it gives rise to a mind of delusion (*moha*), it is the opposite of the aforementioned mind of filial piety.
Furthermore, being unfilial toward one's teacher and disrespectful toward one's elders, and moreover lacking respect, is called *mada* (arrogance); being self-important is called *māna* (pride).
Because one possesses such arrogance and pride, it is termed "delusion. This concludes the section on contrary conduct. As for not rising to welcome or prostrating:
This is the characteristic of contrary conduct.
Each and every item is not in accordance with the Dharma.
There are two [points]: first, regarding each of the six preceding stages, one fails to provide proper offerings and so forth to each individual; second, [the failure to do so] in both cases.
Among all necessary items, each one is not equal to the Dharma. Furthermore, generally speaking, there are five kinds of offerings:
first, physical action (*kāyakarman*), such as welcoming and prostrating; second, verbal action (*vākkarman*), such as praising and expressing humility;
third, mental action (*manaskarman*), which is the mind of respect and filial piety; fourth, things, namely the seven treasures and various objects; and fifth, [the aforementioned three actions].
The Dharma-offering consists of upholding, reciting, and practicing according to the Dharma. In this current passage, there is no mention of verbal action or the Dharma-offering;
however, if one were to apply the general principle of the preceding and following contexts, all five types of offerings would be complete.
If one is truly impoverished and lacks material wealth for offering, there is never an allowance for remaining empty-handed without making an offering; rather, one may even sell oneself to do so.
This applies to both the lay and monastic stages. Regarding the selling of the kingdom and the city: what is governed by the king is called the "kingdom," and what is occupied is called the "city.
As for the selling of men and women, these are the men and women from his original vow; therefore, there is no fault in selling them at that time.
Furthermore, because this Bodhisattva’s profound vows and practices are so deep, he breaks through the bonds of birth-and-death and affection within those very bonds of affection.

Because one dwells in equanimity and is without attachment, one accomplishes the practice and vows by "selling" sons and daughters; (the two preceding positions concern the lay bodhisattva who, through courageous resolve, upholds the precept of non-attachment, and thus "sells" the kingdom, city, sons, and daughters).

Regarding the seven treasures, there are two types: first, the seven treasures consisting of the golden wheel, the jade woman, the horse, the elephant, the pearl, the jade, the military minister, and the treasury minister;
[with these] seven treasures and ten dedications, the bodhisattva becomes a worldly golden-wheel-turning king (cakravartin).

The four continents were first all acquired and later all relinquished, thereby accomplishing the precept of non-attachment. Furthermore, as for the seven treasures: first, gold; second, silver; third, lapis lazuli;

fourth, crystal; fifth, red pearls; sixth, musaragalva; and seventh, agate. (These seven treasures—having already been shown to kings of minor principalities during the stages of the ten faiths, the ten abidings, and the ten practices—are relinquished without attachment by those who have accomplished the vows and practices of a bodhisattva, thereby accomplishing the precept of non-attachment.)
Regarding "all things":
this refers to providing everything that exists, or supplying whatever the Dharma Master requires;

whether by selling or exchanging goods, one must exert every effort to provide them without any stinginess or regret, so that through this total provision, one spontaneously fulfills the bodhisattva's practices and vows.
If it were not so, the commentary states:
"This is the third offense of violating the regulations. It says that if one does not exert full effort in making offerings to the Dharma Master, one will become stingy with wealth and treasures;
this is unless one is personally free from defilement and attachment toward material things, possessing pure vows and precepts."

Although this constitutes an offense, it contradicts one's original vow; therefore, it is classified as a minor defilement (*āpatti-dukkaṭa*). If it is actually associated with stinginess, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
"Minor" refers to what is thin, while "heavy" refers to what is deepened. Whether the transgression is light or heavy can be understood according to the state of the mind.
(The section on failing to provide for one's teachers and elders concludes here.)
▲ The Second Precept: Not to Drink Alcohol. Textual Analysis in Seven Sections: 1. The Intent of the Regulation; 2. The Sequence of the Precept;
3. Explanation of the Name; 4. Requisite Conditions; 5. Deficiency of Conditions; 6. Gravity and Lightness of Offense; 7. General Applicability and Exclusions.
Regarding the original intent of the regulation: Alcohol is the root of delusion and madness, and it causes harm; all manner of faults and calamities arise from alcohol.

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are thirty-six faults in drinking alcohol. It can cause one to commit the four heinous crimes, with the sole exception of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
Since its harm is so extreme, it must be specifically prohibited and severed. (The intent of the regulation concluded.)
Regarding the sequence: the preceding precept prohibited failing to provide for others from the outside; this present precept prohibits internal confusion and distraction.
Thus, the sequence is clarified (the section on sequence concludes).

Third, regarding the explanation of the name: "drinking" (*pāna*) is that which can prevent [intoxication], and "alcohol" (*madya*) is that which is prevented. Because both the agent and the object are involved, the name was established as such.
The Precept Against Drinking Alcohol (the explanation of the name is complete).
Regarding the four conditions that constitute an offense, there are four factors that bring about the violation: first, it must be alcohol; second, one must perceive it as alcohol;

third, one must not be suffering from a grave illness (*Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: "If all other medicines cannot cure it, and a physician says only alcohol can cure it, then it is permitted"); and fourth, swallowing even a single drop of alcohol constitutes an offense.

Since the various Vinayas of the Hīnayāna do not permit [the offense] based on the conditions of mistaken perception or doubt regarding this matter, and because there must be the perception that it is liquor, the present text states: "If a Buddha’s disciple intentionally drinks alcohol," which makes it clear that one commits the offense only when there is the perception that it is liquor.

Regarding the five absences of conditions (*pratyaya-vaikalya*): if any one of the four aforementioned conditions is absent, the offense is either entirely waived and there is no transgression, or even if a transgression occurs, it is light.
(The section on the absence of conditions concludes.

Sixth, regarding the gravity of the offense (*laghu-guru*), there are three aspects: first, in relation to the object (*viṣaya*); second, in relation to the mind (*citta*); and third, a combined analysis. First, in relation to the object:

Regarding the alcohol—whether it be strong, mild, thin, or diluted (concluding the section on the object)—as for the second point concerning the mind: this refers to whether the drinker consumes a small amount or a large amount, for a short time or a long time;

furthermore, within each instance of time, whether it be a small portion, a large portion, or the entirety; and within each of these portions, whether one drinks alone, teaches others to drink, praises it, or rejoices in it.
For each such mental state, the karma resulting from the gravity or lightness of the intention differs accordingly. (Concluding the section on the mind)
[End] Three combinations are distinguished as previously explained through the fourfold application of mind and object.

First, drinking alcohol for a long duration with a defiled mind directed toward all types of alcoholic objects (this karma is most grave). Second, drinking for a short duration with a mind directed toward a limited object (this karma is lightest).
Third, drinking for both a long and a short duration with a mind directed toward both good and bad objects (this karma is intermediate). Fourth, neither a long nor a short duration.

When the mind encounters an object that is not liquor (this refers to the constant association of the mind with the indeterminate [avyākṛta], which may also be termed "maintaining the precepts" and being "without transgression"), one should apply the same principles by analogy to the four permutations of drinking it oneself,
instructing others to drink it, and so forth (the analysis of light and heavy offenses is concluded).
Regarding the seventh point on penetration and obstruction: it is as cited above from the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*.

Furthermore, it refers to cases where one saves others from the peril of losing their lives or from the peril of losing one’s own life; or where, for the sake of preserving life, one accomplishes the conduct of a bodhisattva.

It is also like the case in the *Mallikā-bhāryā-sūtra*, where, in order to save a person who had committed an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*), [the Buddha] drank together with him to cause his heavy karmic burden to be relieved.
In all these cases, the principle is one of open passage and there is no transgression.
Furthermore, it is because the Bodhisattva regards the illnesses of sentient beings as his own illness that when the illnesses of sentient beings are cured, his own illness is likewise cured.

Only a son of the Buddha who possesses the resolve to conceal his own mind in each instance can practice such conduct of illness without defilement or attachment; only then may one proceed. (The section on Passages and Obstructions concludes.)
"If a Buddha's disciple intentionally consumes alcohol and thereby gives rise to the immeasurable faults of intoxication...

[The Commentator] states: This passage on abstaining from alcohol is divided into three parts: first, citing the faults of alcohol (the text reads "intentionally consuming alcohol" down to "immeasurable," which is this section).

Second, the manifestation of the transgression (the text says: "If one personally takes it down [to others] so that sentient beings drink alcohol, this is it"). Third, the formal conclusion of the offense for violating the regulation (the text says:

"If one intentionally drinks it oneself," and so forth). Regarding the first [point], concerning those who raise the issue of the transgression: since this sūtra has been transmitted for a long time, there are editions that read, "If one intentionally serves alcohol, one gives rise to immeasurable faults of alcohol";
furthermore, there are editions that add the character "good" (*śubha*) to read, "one loses [a good state]."
Regarding "immeasurable wholesome [roots]" (which the student should know), it is because the present explanation relies on the statement that one loses immeasurable roots of goodness;
therefore, among the offenses arising from delusion, drinking alcohol is excluded as it does not constitute such a loss.
Regarding the loss of immeasurable merit:
because of excessive transgressions, all wholesome roots are lost.
This includes if one personally passes a vessel of alcohol to another, or even down to providing it for any sentient being to drink.
The commentary states: This second section on the manifestation of transgressions is divided into two parts: first, the manifestation of the transgression regarding the passing of wine vessels;

second, the manifestation of the transgression regarding drinking wine. Now, for the first: "If one passes a wine vessel with one's own hand to another so that they drink the wine, they shall be without hands for five hundred lifetimes.
This cites a minor offense to illustrate a major one, and a shallow case to exemplify a profound one; passing the vessel constitutes the minor offense.

Even this minor offense results in being without hands for five hundred lifetimes; if one drinks it oneself or teaches others to drink it, one will certainly fall into the hells for many kalpas, let alone drinking *li* wine.
How much more so for drinking it oneself, down to the point of any sentient being drinking alcohol.
The commentary states: This second section on the characteristics of the actual offense uses light cases to illustrate heavy ones;

while the text lacks explicit mention of praising or rejoicing [in the act], such a principle exists implicitly. (The characteristics of the fault regarding alcohol are as explained previously in the precept against selling alcohol.)
If one intentionally drinks [alcohol], down to the level of a minor offense of defilement, the commentary states:
This third point concerns the violation of the regulations that constitutes an offense. The Sūtra says that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and are all capable of receiving the precepts;
yet, if one teaches others to drink alcohol, it causes them to become dazed and insane, thereby obstructing their clear and penetrating wisdom.
It is for this reason that alcohol is prohibited (the precept against drinking alcohol concludes).
▲ The Third Precept: Not Eating Meat; Textual Exposition, Part One of Seven Gates (as above).
Regarding the original intent of the regulation: Generally speaking, one who is a bodhisattva ought only to sacrifice their own flesh to save the lives of all beings.
How could they permit the severing of the seeds of great compassion and act as an enemy to sentient beings by consuming the blood and flesh of others? Such irrationality is extreme;
therefore, this regulation was established. (The intent of the regulation concludes.)

Regarding the sequence: since the preceding [section] concerned abstaining from intoxicants that cause confusion, and the present [section] concerns abstaining from food that harms life, it follows in this order.
(End of Sequence). Third, regarding the explanation of the names:
"Son of the Buddha" refers to the person who eats, and "flesh and blood" refers to the flavors that are eaten; thus the name is established.
It is called the "precept against eating meat" because it is established to prevent this [transgression] (the explanation of the name is complete).

Regarding the four conditions for its completion, there are four: first, it must be meat (for if it is not meat, there is no offense); second, it must be the meat of another (for eating one's own flesh does not constitute a formal offense);
third, one must perceive it as meat (for if there is a mistake, there is no offense); and fourth, it must enter the mouth to complete the offense (the explanation of the conditions is complete).

Regarding the five absences of conditions (*pratyaya-vaidhurya*): as explained above under the section on conditions, if any one of the conditions is absent or if the offense is minor, there is no transgression; this may be understood [as the conclusion of the section on absent conditions].

Sixth, regarding lightness and gravity (*laghu-guru*), there are three divisions: first, based on the object (*viṣaya*); second, based on the mind (*citta*); third, a combined analysis. First, concerning the object:
There are four types of meat that are equivalent [to forbidden meat]: first, all fetal membranes are "meat without life"; second, the remains of birds and beasts that have died naturally;

third, "pure meat" (which, according to the teachings of the Hīnayāna, refers to meat not seen, not heard, and not suspected to have been killed for one's sake); and fourth, meat obtained through seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing that it was specifically slaughtered for oneself.

Regarding the transgressions involved in these four types, they are discussed together in terms of karma: as the objects [of the offense] progress from the first to the last, the gravity of the resulting karma increases accordingly. (The section on the object concludes. Second.
Regarding the mind: within the category of unwholesome minds, one distinguishes between those of brief duration, long duration, and extended duration, such as the mind that eats meat.
Within each of these instances, one further distinguishes between partial, majority, and total consumption of meat.

Within each of these divisions, there are various mental states, such as eating for oneself, encouraging others to eat, or rejoicing in it. One should reflect upon the gravity of the karma created by such mental states.

Regarding the resolution of these [concluding the section on "Constraining the Mind"]: as for the comparative analysis of the three mental objects (*citta-viṣaya*), the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) concerning lightness and heaviness are to be understood as explained previously regarding the gravity of the offense incurred [concluding the comparative analysis].

Regarding the seventh point, "penetration and obstruction": this refers to those at the stage of the Three Worthies (*trayaḥ pūrvayogāḥ*) in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-dharma*). Because they do not perceive the spiritual capacity [of sentient beings], their practice is entirely obstructed.

From the First Ground (*prathamabhūmi*) upward, they perceive the capacity and act accordingly; or, for the sake of causes and conditions such as eating meat, they cause sentient beings to give rise to the aspiration of a Bodhisattva and achieve the Bodhisattva mind.
By severing evil and generating good, and by destroying delusions and perceiving the principle, they ought to perform such acts.
(The practice of penetration and obstruction is concluded).
As for the passage beginning "If a Buddha’s disciple eats meat," the commentary states:
this section on the precept against eating meat is divided into three parts: first, stating the reason for not eating meat (the text says, "following the Buddha...").

[The disciple] descends [in his argument] to the point that one must not eat the flesh of any sentient being. Second, it clarifies that eating meat incurs immeasurable offenses (the text states this in the passage beginning with "a single spoonful").
Third, it addresses the violation of the precept and the resulting transgression (the text states, "if one intentionally eats it, one commits a minor offense").

Now, for the first [section], there are two parts: first, presenting the rationale for not eating meat (from the beginning up to "and abandon it"); second, the prohibition itself (the text states, "all Bodhisattvas must not eat the flesh of any sentient being"). Regarding the first part, the introductory heading is established as follows:
"One must not eat meat" means that, as stated in the text, no kind of meat whatsoever may be eaten. Next, the meaning of the prohibition against eating meat is explained:

[The fourth precept on] "Not eating the five pungent roots" (the fifth text), with its seven preceding sections (as above).

How could there be the consumption of the five pungent roots, whose foul odors and stench would defile the worthy sages and benevolent deities?
Since these spirits would abandon them and malevolent ghosts would seize their place, it was necessary to establish this regulation. (The intent concluded.)

Regarding the sequence: the preceding precept restricts the possession of life within the constituent parts of the body, whereas this precept restricts the five pungent herbs which are devoid of life;
therefore, it follows in sequence. (End of Sequence).

Third, regarding the explanation of the name: the Buddha’s disciples who are capable of consuming [the forbidden] constitute the "agent of prevention," while the various types of five pungent plants constitute the "object of prevention.
Because the established rule prohibits and cuts them off, it is called the precept of not eating the five pungent plants.

Furthermore, evil habits and sensual desires constitute the "agent of prevention," while the categories of aromatic and pungent plants constitute the "object of prevention. Because both agent and object are regulated, it is called the precept of not eating the five pungent plants.

(End of Names). Fourth, the four conditions for the offense: first, the five pungent herbs; second, the perception that they are such; third, the absence of an opening condition (such as a grave illness where life must be saved, or seeing an opportunity to save a being);
fourth, the moment they enter the mouth, one commits the offense. (End of Conditions).

Regarding the five absences of conditions: as with the four conditions mentioned above, if each one is absent, the precept is light and there is no offense; this is easily understood. (End of Absence of Conditions) Regarding the six categories of light and heavy:

based on the object, there are the distinctions of "raw" versus "ripe"; based on the vital energy, there are the distinctions of "dull" versus "flourishing"; based on the mind, there are the distinctions of "joy" versus "aversion," or "attachment" versus "equanimity.
These three times, three portions, and four stages may be understood by analogy with what preceded. (End of Light and Heavy)

Seventh, regarding the open and the obstructed: if one is personally afflicted by illness and there is no medicine to treat it, yet one perceives an opportunity to save a life, bringing benefit and peace, then it is logically appropriate that all such cases be open;
except for these specific circumstances, all others are obstructed. (The section on the open and the obstructed concludes.)
"If a Buddha’s disciple does not eat the five pungent plants...
[The commentary] states: This is precisely the text for the precept against eating the five pungent plants, which is divided into three parts:

first, the designation that one must not eat the five pungent plants (from the beginning up to "hingukā"); second, the formal proclamation of the prohibition (from "these five kinds" up to "must not eat"); third, the conclusion regarding the violation of the rule.

Regarding the transgressions (from "if one intentionally eats" down to "is a violation," this is it): now, first, in the section on abstaining from food, there is first the heading of the five pungent vegetables (*pañca-garaka*), followed by the enumeration of their five types.
