In other places, there are different lists where leek (*śunaka*), garlic (*laśuna*), onion (*palāṇḍu*), *kārilla*, and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) constitute the five [forbidden vegetables]. In the present sutra, the term "onion" (*palaṇḍu*) has been revised; according to tradition, this refers to the mountain onion (*śaila-palaṇḍu*).
Those who dwell in the mountains say it is more pungent than the onions found among humans. As for "compassionate onion" (*maitrī-palaṇḍu*), this is the Persian onion (*hūna-palaṇḍu*).
As for "orchid onion" (*uraga-palaṇḍu*), this refers to that which is cultivated in the gardens of common households. Regarding *kārilla*, some explain it as *yūn* (cumin).
Regarding *rāī*, some say it is the medicinal plant *hiṅgu* (asafoetida), while others say it is naturally found in the mountains of Hainan;
its pungent stench makes it difficult to approach. As for garlic (*laśuna*), it is commonly eaten by people, as is well known. (And so forth.)
Regarding these five kinds of food that must not be eaten among all types of food:
the commentary states that this is the second formal proclamation establishing the prohibition.
If one should intentionally eat what has fallen [to the ground], [it is a transgression].
The commentary states: This is the third offense of transgressing a prescribed rule (the precept against eating the five pungent herbs is concluded).
▲ The fifth precept: "One must not fail to instruct another on their confessed offense," consisting of seven sections as before (same as above).

The original intent of this precept is as follows: O Disciples of the Buddha, if you see anyone who has violated the precepts, you should employ skillful means to instruct and exhort them to repent so that they may return to their original state of purity.
This is precisely what constitutes benefiting oneself and others, and ensuring that the True Dharma endures for a long time.
Yet, if you instead abandon the four immeasurable minds and forsake your fundamental vows, failing to teach all offenders to repent, you commit an offense.
To dwell together while sharing the same interests causes the dust and grime of the Dharma-gates to accumulate; when the meaning of the Dharma is impaired, one’s own practice fails to achieve purity.
When the three groups of sentient beings share the same activities, the correct cause cannot be established, and the principle of gathering and transforming living beings becomes distorted.
Since this is not the conduct of a Bodhisattva, it was necessary for the Sage to establish these prohibitions. (The intent concluded.)
Regarding the sequence: previously, one purified one’s own person; now, this precept is established next to prohibit associating with those who engage in impure and evil conduct. (End of Sequence).

Third, regarding the explanation of the name: all violations of the precepts are termed "having offense," yet for a bodhisattva not to instruct others to repent their transgressions is termed "lack of compassion.

Since this results in neither self nor others being pure, and because the precept of identical activity prevents this fault, it is called the "precept of not instructing others to repent their offenses.
Furthermore, O sons of the Buddha, if one does not teach and instruct all beings with compassion, it is termed "not instructing them to repent."
Thus, for all who violate the precepts and thereby manifest evil causes in the present that will inevitably result in evil fruits in the future, this regulation was established to prevent such acts;
hence it is called the "precept against failing to instruct others to repent their transgressions. (End of section on names.)
The four conditions for the concealment [of an offense] consist of five factors: first, the sentient being has committed an infraction; second, one knows that they have committed an offense;

third, there is no other exceptional circumstance permitting its disclosure; fourth, one conceals their offense due to a lack of compassion; and fifth, one conceals it for the sake of sharing common benefits of the Dharma (the section on the conditions is complete).
Regarding the five deficiencies of conditions: if any one of the aforementioned conditions is lacking, there is no offense, even if it is minor (end of section on deficiencies).

Regarding the six categories of light and heavy offenses: for those who have committed an offense against the five precepts or the eight precepts, if one does not instruct them to repent, the fault is termed "light.

For those who have committed an offense against the ten precepts, the full set of precepts, or the seven heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), if one does not instruct them to repent, they will suffer for long kalpas; this [failure to guide them] further constitutes a transgression against the Bodhisattva path.

Because compassion is profound, it is weighty. Furthermore, if one were to judge all phenomena through reasoning as being equal, yet the precepts differentiate according to circumstances, then a Bodhisattva would be violating reason;

thus, [the Buddha] does not teach that one must repent for everything. As in the present case, when the precepts are established, each instance of transgression constitutes a minor defilement (light dust).
(The section on light and heavy offenses concludes.)

Seventh, regarding penetration and obstruction: if one lacks the five virtues or the ten virtues oneself, others will not believe or comply; thus, while the principle is penetrated, there is no transgression.

However, if one actually possesses these virtues but, out of a frivolous mind or a conceited mind, does not instruct them to repent their faults, this constitutes an obstruction due to a lack of compassion. (The section on penetration and obstruction is concluded.)
"If a disciple of the Buddha [sees] any sentient being who has violated even the lowest of the eight precepts...
[The commentary states: This section on the precept against failing to teach the repentance of transgressions is divided into three parts:

first, the introduction stating that all who have violated the precepts should be taught to repent (from the beginning up to "should be taught to repent"); second, the exposition of the common rule regarding not teaching repentance (from "therefore, the Bodhisattva" ...).

"Reaching the assembly's dwelling for the recitation of the precepts" constitutes the third violation of the regulations leading to an offense (from "yet failing to raise [the issue]" to "committing an offense").

Now, first, the characteristics of all offenses are enumerated (from the beginning up to "all offenses of violating the precepts"). Next, one should instruct them in repentance (the text is as in the topical outline). Now, regarding the first:

these three types of precepts—the eight precepts, the five precepts, and the ten precepts—if received within the Lesser Vehicle, apply to both monastics and laypeople; once these have been received, they are above that.
The ten precepts are identical to the ten wholesome precepts; therefore, if one takes the ten precepts as the śrāmaṇera precepts, they pertain solely to the monastic path and not to the laity.
Furthermore, these ten grave precepts of the present sutra may be received by all beings throughout the six realms. Regarding those who violate the prohibitions:

among the ten śrāmaṇera precepts, violating the prohibitions against killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitutes a breach for a bhikṣu, while violating the prohibition against intoxicants constitutes a breach for a bhikṣuṇī. Thus, there are four grave offenses for a bhikṣu and eight for a bhikṣuṇī.

In this sutra, those who commit the ten grave offenses are all termed "violators of prohibitions" (and so forth). Furthermore, the violation of any prescribed precept—regardless of whether it is light or heavy—is termed "violation of prohibitions.
Regarding the seven heinous crimes (*saptānantarya*), they are explained as follows in the subsequent section on the precepts.

Regarding the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*), ancient masters state that these are the three miserable realms (*tri-durgati*) and the five [remaining] difficulties. [Commentary: These eight difficulties are the places where beings in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) undergo retribution.
Since this is not the cause for confessing by means of exposing one's faults, it is not employed here;

rather, according to the exposition in the *Bodhisattva-bhūmi-śīla-sūtra*, the bodhisattva precepts consist of eight grave rules (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*), which are largely identical to the ten major precepts of the present sutra.

If a bodhisattva violates these eight grave rules, they will be reborn in the eight difficult states (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*); thus, by taking the causes of these eight grave offenses and eight difficult states as the basis, the bodhisattva is made to expose their faults and perform confession.
Because the cause is explained by means of its fruit, it is called one of the eight difficulties (aṣṭāvakṣaṇa), and so forth.

Regarding the statement that all transgressions of the precepts should be taught as requiring repentance (*pratideśanā*), the commentary states: "This section clarifies those cases where one should be taught to repent," and so forth.

Yet, a Bodhisattva does not instruct [others] to perform repentance while dwelling together with them, sharing the same monastic community and its benefits, and participating in the *poṣadha* as a single assembly for the recitation of the precepts.
The commentary states:
This second point clarifies that which a Bodhisattva should do and what they should not do; specifically, one should not instruct [others] to perform repentance in such a manner.
"And they dwell together, share the same Saṃgha, share the same benefits, and recite the precepts together... (and so forth). Question:
For those who have received the five precepts or the eight precepts, as these are laypeople, where can they dwell together with Bodhisattvas, share the same benefits, and recite the precepts?
Answer: There are two interpretations of this. First, those who have merely received the five or eight precepts do not delight in hearing about the Bodhisattva [path]. [...]
Regarding the Bodhisattva precepts, the Tathāgata asked about not dwelling together with those who do not observe the precepts when reciting them.

If there are sentient beings whose minds have faith and inclination toward the Mahāyāna, yet find it difficult to receive the five or eight precepts while desiring to hear the great Bodhisattva precepts, the Buddha has granted permission for this;
therefore, the preceding text states that anyone who possesses a heart directed toward the precepts and understands the Dharma Master’s words may all receive the precepts.
All are called those of supreme purity. Furthermore, the *Benye jing* (Sūtra on Original Karma) states:

"A Bodhisattva Dharma Master first recites and explains [the teachings] for that person, causing their mind to open and their understanding to be clarified; only then does he confer the precepts upon them.
Therefore, even those who have received only the five or eight precepts may dwell together with Bodhisattvas and participate in the recitation of the precepts (and so forth).
*Poṣadha* (布薩):
This is translated as "nurturing and purifying the Dharma. The Buddha commanded his disciples to examine themselves and their minds every half-month.
If there have been transgressions of the precepts, they should feel shame and repent. Because this nurtures and brings to fulfillment pure and virtuous conduct, it is called *poṣadha*.
[Sa... (and so forth). Yet he does not cite their offenses, down to those who have committed an offense. The commentary states:

This is the third violation of the regulations (*vaiśeṣika-dharma*), namely the offense of [failing to] instruct [them] to repent for their transgressions (the meaning of the precept on failing to admonish repentance is concluded).
▲ Section Six on the Necessity of Providing [Offerings] for Requesting the Dharma and Precepts (same as above).
The first part, regarding the intent of the regulation, is as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma.
Because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal; therefore, all Buddhas offer worship, reverence, respect, and honor [to the Dharma]."
The reason for this praise is that the Dharma resides in the person who honors it;

because the person upholds the Dharma, they abandon arrogance and eliminate haughtiness, traveling hundreds or thousands of *li* to welcome and escort [the teacher], inviting the Dharma at the six times of the day, even to the point of sacrificing their own bodies for the sake of the Dharma.
Yet, the Bodhisattva instead indulges in arrogance, giving rise to a mind of affliction and distress, being haughty toward others and treating the Dharma with contempt.
Because the loss of the benefits of the Dharma is so grave, it must be regulated (the intent is concluded).
Regarding the second explanation, which combines the latter term: being shrouded by stinginess and entangled by self-conceit, one fails to provide for others;

because of this, one treats people with contempt and disregards the Dharma, thus failing to invite [the Sangha]. Out of great compassion, the Great Sage established the precepts to prevent this; therefore, it is called "failing to provide" and "not inviting the Dharma."

Precepts are also called the "precepts against disrespecting persons. The Dharma does not function in isolation; its propagation depends upon people, yet people cannot achieve fulfillment on their own—they must rely on the Dharma to establish themselves.
Because one harbors pride, self-importance, and arrogance, it is called "disrespect for the Dharma";
because one is stingy regarding what is required, it is called "not honoring persons. Thus, the path of the Dharma is blocked by parsimony and pride; the precepts prevent these failings.
Therefore, it is called "Disrespect for the Dharma and Contempt for Persons and Precepts" (end of title).

Regarding the sequence: because the preceding precept concerns failing to instruct one who has committed an offense to repent, and this present precept concerns slighting persons of virtue and being arrogant toward the Dharma, they arise in this successive order (end of sequence).

The four conditions for this transgression are: first, being a practitioner who adheres to the Mahāyāna view; second, the absence of any special cause for exemption; third, the arising of a mind of stinginess or pride;
and fourth, failing to make offerings or request the Dharma—this constitutes the offense. (The section on the conditions is concluded.)
Regarding the five deficiencies of conditions: if it concerns those of the Hīnayāna who hold differing views and follow different practices, then the first condition is deficient;
as for other deficiencies of conditions, they may be understood [as previously explained]. (End of section on deficiencies).

Sixth, regarding the gravity [of the offense], there are three categories based on the person: 1. If one has already mastered the practice and conduct (*śikṣā*) to the extent that they are fit to serve as a model for others, yet fails to respectfully invite them [to teach], this is grave.

2. If the other person’s mastery of practice and conduct is equal to one’s own, yet one fails to respectfully invite them, this is slightly less grave. 3. If the other person’s mastery of practice and conduct is inferior to one’s own, there is no offense.

(End of section on persons) Regarding the category of the teaching (*dharma*): if it is a Mahāyāna sūtra or vinaya that truly teaches the permanence [of the Buddha-nature], yet one does not respectfully [engage with it]...

If one requests [teachings] while being heavy with pride, the offense is grave; if the persons requesting are divided equally between those who understand both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna and those who understand only half of each, the offense is slightly lighter due to their lack of reverence;
if they understand and practice only the Hīnayāna but do not understand the Mahāyāna, there is no offense. (The section on the Dharma concludes.)

Seventh, regarding penetration and obstruction: if a bodhisattva has developed the wisdom-eye and the dharma-eye, they know the timely and the untimely, skillfully recognize individuals, and penetrate the principles of the Dharma without transgression.

Since everything remains obstructed for those who have not yet reached this stage, even the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions who are in their final birth before Buddhahood all request the Dharma from them. (The section on Penetration and Obstruction concludes.)
"If a disciple of the Buddha sees a Great Vehicle Dharma Master of lower status...

[The commentary states: This section on the precept regarding providing for and requesting the Dharma from others is divided into three parts: first, clarifying the conditions for establishing the precept (from the beginning up to "those who come from a thousand *li*");

second, correctly clarifying the establishment of the precept (from "immediately rising" up to "requesting the Dharma even at the cost of one's life"); third, concluding with the offense for violating the regulation (if one does not do so...).
"This is now the first time I have seen a Dharma Master of the Mahāyāna" is a general designation for those who study the Mahāyāna as distinct from the Hīnayāna.
"Those of the Mahāyāna who share the same views and the same practices."
Because the practices of those who study the Mahāyāna differ, and because they differ, this text separately selects and extracts those whose views and practices are identical;
such individuals should be invited to enter monasteries, residences, cities, and towns, and provided with offerings.
Those who come from a hundred or a thousand *li* do so because they clearly intend to propagate the Great Dharma; thus, they travel great distances to receive its transmission.
This includes rising to welcome them and seeing them off, down to those who exhaust their very lives in requesting the Dharma.
The commentary states: This second section concerns the formal establishment of the precepts on the day of the ritual.
Because the request for the Dharma involves persons of high standing, the most precious among valuables—gold—is cited. Therefore, it says one should provide offerings of three *liang* of gold daily.

Furthermore, because the Dharma Master transmits the teachings in place of the Buddha to expound the Buddha’s instructions, he consumes these offerings as if he were the Buddha himself, according to the *Bhagavad-vimokṣa-sūtra*.
It is stated therein that the offense of slandering the Buddha is light, whereas the offense of slandering a Dharma teacher is heavy;

yet the "Dharma Teacher" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that if one makes offerings to a Dharma teacher, it is equivalent to making offerings to the Buddha. Furthermore, if a person were to slander the Buddha for an entire kalpa, the offense would still be relatively light;
however, if a person were to revile for even a brief moment one who upholds, recites, and studies the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the offense is exceedingly grave. This is because...
This is spoken because the Buddha, throughout various Mahāyāna sūtras, has taught that one should revere the Dharma and honor those who uphold it as something unprecedented.
For example, in the *Adbhutadharmaparyāya*, the devas removed their celestial robes and fine garments to serve as a seat and invited the jackal-preceptor (*śṛgāla-upādhyāya*) to preach the Dharma;
and in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the youth of the Snowy Mountains promised to sacrifice his own body and life in order to seek even half a verse, offering it as an act of worship.
In the *Rākṣasamahāparivarta-sūtra*, it is recounted how the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita struck his own bones to seek the Prajñāpāramitā;

such accounts describe how bodhisattvas revere the Dharma and honor others, not begrudging even their own bodies or lives. Thus, the passage in this sutra concerning sacrificing one's body for the sake of the Dharma and requesting the teaching is precisely this.
Regarding the statement, "One should offer worship three times daily, request the Dharma Master to preach the Dharma three times, and perform prostrations three times," the commentary states:
For one who is a bodhisattva, before having personally realized the true *dharmakāya* and before establishing oneself in the stages (*bhūmi*), it is logically appropriate that doubts may arise;
thus, upon hearing or seeing something superior, one should simply request [instruction]. Why limit the frequency to three or six times?
Having entered the first bhūmi and above, one asks the Buddhas of the ten directions and the great bodhisattvas regarding all dharmas and their meanings within every single thought-moment.
Regarding these three periods: for those established in the forty stages of mind, it is not yet permitted to inquire about the Dharma and request instruction in every thought-moment;
therefore, it is prescribed that one does so during the three periods of each day and night—namely, morning, midday, and afternoon. "This very day" refers to the beginning of the period.
Because it is after midnight, it is called the "third period. Residing in the stage of an ordinary person, one restrains oneself so as not to give rise to anger or a mind of affliction;
this is requesting the Dharma at the cost of sacrificing one's own body.
If it were not so, [the commentary] states:
"This is the third offense of transgressing a regulation (a grave offense for disrespecting the Dharma and those worthy of honor; the precept on failing to provide service is hereby concluded)."
▲ Section Seven: Not to Be Indolent or Refuse to Listen to the Dharma and Precepts (The same as above for the first seven sections).

First, regarding the intent of the regulation: All sons of the Buddha should uphold the Sūtras and Vinaya and proceed to places where the Dharma is being expounded to listen, receive, inquire, and seek instruction, thereby nourishing their own spirits, increasing their wisdom, and perfecting the Dharma-body and the life of insight; yet, they instead remain indolent and lazy.

[The intention behind the prohibition is concluded as follows: Because going where one should not go and listening to what one should not hear increase one’s own ignorance and diminish the life of wisdom, the Noble One (the Buddha) laboriously established this rule.
Second, regarding the sequence: the preceding precept required requesting the Great Dharma, while the present precept requires listening to the Great Dharma; therefore, it follows in sequence.
[The sequential order is concluded].

Third, regarding the explanation of the name: there are places where the Dharma is taught where the physical and mental dispositions for upholding the Dharma have become indolent, and people do not go to listen or receive it.

To prevent this fault, the Sage established a precept to restrain them; therefore, it is called the "Precept Against Indolence and Not Listening to the Dharma. [The explanation of the name is concluded].
The four conditions for this offense are as follows: first, one is a beginner; second, there is a place where the Dharma is being preached; third, there is no other extenuating circumstance;
and fourth, if one does not go to listen and receive the teaching, one commits the offense. (The section on the conditions is concluded.)
The five cases of missing conditions may be understood by analogy with what precedes (end of "missing conditions").
Sixth, regarding gravity: there are three categories based on the person. First, those who lecture on both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; second, those who lecture on the Mahāyāna but not the Hīnayāna;

third, those who lecture on the Hīnayāna but not the Mahāyāna. Of these, the first two are grave, while for the latter, there may be no offense. This applies if one has received the *vinaya* of majestic deportment from the Tathāgata.
Because there are still transgressions even after the prohibitions have been established (concluding the section on light and heavy).

Seventh, regarding penetration and obstruction: if one knows for oneself that the wisdom-life of the *dharmakāya* has already been established, then penetration occurs while all else is obstructed (concluding the section on penetration and obstruction).
"If there is a place anywhere where the Dharma and Vinaya are being preached, and one is of lower status," etc.

The commentary states: This precept against indolence regarding the failure to listen to the Dharma is divided into three parts: first, citing the occasion for the precept (from the beginning up to "where the Dharma is being preached");

second, the formal regulation (from "Now, the newly initiated Bodhisattva" up to "listen and receive it"); third, the conclusion regarding the offense for violating the regulation (from "If one does not go" onwards). Now, the first part.

Regarding the statement that "wherever there is the teaching of the Dharma, Vinaya, Sūtras, and Śāstras," the commentary says: "Teaching the Dharma" refers to the two studies (śikṣā) which collectively encompass all Buddha-dharmas.

"Vinaya" is translated here as "extinction" (nirodha); it is capable of extinguishing the afflictions of the five abodes (pañca-vāsika-kleśa)—which is the meaning of "extinguishing" as taught in the Mahāyāna, namely the extinction of all afflictions.
If one speaks of the Small Vehicle, the outflow-tainted *mokṣa* (prātimokṣa) is capable of extinguishing the seven branches of body and speech.

"Evil is called 'extinguished' (this explains it in terms of the precepts of majestic power). If one possesses the precepts co-arising with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the precepts co-arising with the Path (*mārga*), one can extinguish the ninety-eight afflictions (this refers to the untainted precepts of the Hīnayāna).
As for the Sūtras and Vinaya, they encompass all Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas.
If a Bodhisattva clearly understands that his own body possesses the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), then according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he abides in true wisdom."
One who employs wisdom through skillful means does not contradict any of the Hīnayāna;
although they study the Hīnayāna, they know it is subsumed within the Buddha’s skillful wisdom for the purpose of guiding a certain class of beings, and that they ultimately return to the Mahāyāna.

Thus, by studying the Buddha’s expedient means, they do not violate the subsequent precept against turning one's back on the Mahāyāna to listen to the Hīnayāna. If one does not grasp this meaning, one commits the offense of turning one's back [on the Mahāyāna].
This refers to the Great [Precepts] being directed toward the Small Precepts.

This refers to the text on the precept against divisive speech (*paiśunya*), which is divided into three parts: first, the narrative of the circumstances for establishing the precept (from the beginning up to "Bodhisattva practice").

1) The intention behind the two types of prohibitions (*śikṣāpada*) [is explained] from "thereby engaging in conflict" down to "not committing this. 2) The violation of the prohibition resulting in an offense (*āpatti*) [is explained] from "if done intentionally" onwards.

Now, regarding the first [point], "because of an evil mind" refers to various forms of jealousy, a mind of deceitful contempt, arrogance and competitiveness, a mind of factionalism and attachment to views, a mind that does not reflect upon its own faults, and a mind that constantly litigates the shortcomings of others; such are the characteristics of these entanglements (*paryavasthāna*).
Because all minds should be considered evil:

when one sees someone upholding the precepts and even practicing the bodhisattva path, those with evil minds view this as hypocrisy and slander; therefore, this is the occasion for establishing the prohibitions.
Regarding the phrase "yet those who fail to encounter or visit [the Buddha]," the commentary states:

This is the second intended purpose behind the formulation of the precept; it is because the Buddha’s intention does not permit the practice of divisive speech (*paiśunya*), as it causes both parties to commit evil.
If one intentionally disparages [others], the commentary states:
this is the third offense involving a violation of the regulations (the precept against slandering virtuous people with double-tongued speech ends here).
Next follows the twentieth precept: "One must not fail to rescue sentient beings from suffering" (the text is the same as above).
Regarding the original intent of this precept: when a bodhisattva first resolves to attain enlightenment, they vow to rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
To see others being slaughtered while harboring no heart of rescue or deliverance violates the practice of compassion to an extreme degree; therefore, this precept was established. (End of Intent)
Regarding the sequence: because the preceding precept was established due to the disparagement and slander of those who were virtuous and wise, this present precept is now established.

Seeing beings born into suffering, one fails to rescue them as they fall into it and undergo torment; this is termed "suffering of birth. Because the agent and the object are combined in this designation, it is called the "precept against failing to rescue sentient beings from suffering" (the term "named" concludes).

The four conditions for its completion are: first, lacking internal compassion and succor; second, seeing a person killing; third, abandoning [them] and not rescuing; fourth, [the act of] killing being completed. (The four conditions concluded.)
Saving the four lives, severing [the bonds], and failing to preach the precepts constitute an offense (the full details are concluded).
Fifth, the conditions for deficiency; sixth, lightness and gravity; seventh, penetration and obstruction (to be judged according to the above).
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of a heart of compassion...
The commentary states: This section on the precept of not failing to rescue sentient beings from suffering is divided into three parts:

(1) the regulation on what ought to be done (from the beginning up to "receiving birth after birth"); (2) what ought to be rescued and taught (from "if one sees worldly people" up to "born among humans or in the heavens"); and (3) the conclusion regarding the offense for violating the regulation (from "if one does not...
onwards). Now, for the first part, "what ought to be done": the Bodhisattva, through unconditional compassion (*nirālamba-karuṇā*), contemplates the three realms and the six destinies and abandons...
The bodies of sentient beings and one's own body alike receive the four great elements; if one were to kill another, it would be killing the very essence of one's own body.

Because they share the same nature, the same characteristic, the same substance, the same function, the same practice, the same position, the same cause, and the same fruit—being equal and equal without distinction—the essence of one’s own body is [the same as theirs]. [Because of this,] one continuously performs the karma of taking life.
Regarding "if one sees people of the world," the commentary states:

This second [principle] requires that one both provide rescue and deliver instruction—either rescuing first and instructing later, or instructing first and rescuing later—acting as the situation permits.
The essential point is to rescue them with a mind of compassion, ensuring equality toward both enemies and kin. Therefore...
On the anniversary of the passing of one's parents, one now preaches the precepts for the sake of bestowing the supreme bliss upon all sentient beings;
thus it is said that by resolving their suffering and hardships, they shall be able to behold the Buddhas.
If it were not so, those below [would suffer].
The commentary states: This is the third offense of violating a regulation (the precept on failing to rescue sentient beings from suffering is concluded).
